gotama.notes: Gotama 11 is the Buddha addressed in the DPD examples. Gotama 05 explains his family name. DN 14 repeatedly says gotamo gottena, and in SN 35.243 the Buddha addresses the Sakyans of Kapilavatthu in the plural, gotamā. The chapter summaries at Thag 2.10 and 3.16 name the elders of Thag 2.9 and 3.14 respectively. The attribution and summary at Thag 10.7 agree on the third elder. The tap on that poem’s title Gotamattheragāthā offers only the two earlier poems. Several individuals lack a matching candidate. Vaṅgīsa calls himself Gotama in SN 8.3 and addresses Ānanda in SN 8.4. SN 9.5 names Ānanda as the addressee of the verse also found in Thag 1.119. Thag 17.3 calls Gotama the Buddha’s attendant. In Thag 10.1 Kāḷudāyī addresses Suddhodana, the Buddha’s father. Thag 21.1 contains the verses to Vaṅgīsa himself and to Ānanda as well as praise of the Buddha. Snp 5.19 praises the Buddha and also names a disciple, Gotama of Āḷavī, at 16.2. A single entry would misidentify some taps in each of these last two poems. SN 1.23 and 1.75 give little identifying detail beyond the address to Gotama. SN 7.6 explicitly frames the tangle dialogue also found in SN 1.23. Two missing addresses to the Buddha are Snp 5.5:9.2 and 5.8:7.2. Sujato has ‘Gotama’ in both, while the dictionary splits gotamanūpadhīkaṁ with feminine gotami. The omitted Gotamabharaṇḍuhatthako at AN 3.132:4.2 abbreviates titles in a chapter summary. Its first item points back to the Gotamaka shrine of AN 3.125. Several Gotama 11 citations span neighboring discourses. The delicate upbringing is in AN 3.39, the dreams in AN 5.196, the splinter in SN 1.38, and the solitary retreat in SN 45.11. The corresponding pages also pick up AN 3.38, AN 5.195, SN 1.37 and SN 45.10. Nandiya’s direct address in SN 45.10 independently identifies the Buddha. Check the entry’s MN.i.118ff reference for the first sermon. MN 19 and MN 20 discuss thought, while the discourse to the five at Isipatana is SN 56.11. Claude: SN 1.23:1.3 is a deity addressing the Buddha.
